analysis.one_liner: Bars new IRS enforcement money from auditing taxpayers earning under $400,000.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced September 12, 2022, referred to the Finance Committee, and died there when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 gave the IRS roughly $80 billion over a decade, much of it for enforcement—i.e., audits. This bill would have written a legal prohibition into that law: none of that new money could be spent auditing taxpayers with taxable incomes below $400,000. It was a response to claims that the new funding would unleash an 'army of auditors' on ordinary families. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote or hearing before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, households earning under $400,000 in taxable income would have a statutory guarantee that new IRS enforcement money could not be used to audit them. Wealthy taxpayers and their advisers would also benefit in a subtler way: an audit rate freeze on the bottom 97% of earners would make it harder for the IRS to raise overall audit coverage, since higher-income returns require more examiner hours.

how_it_helps.text: Writes a binding legal restriction into the Inflation Reduction Act: none of the new IRS money could fund audits of taxpayers with taxable incomes below $400,000 [S2][S3].
Responds to public concern, amplified in the debate over the Inflation Reduction Act, that new IRS funding would increase audit pressure on ordinary families rather than on high earners.

analysis.who_pays: If the restriction had passed, the Treasury would have collected less in unpaid taxes: the IRS estimates uncollected taxes, largely from high earners and large partnerships, run into the hundreds of billions a year. Money that Congress had already appropriated to narrow that gap could not have been spent on the audits most likely to find it, because under-resourced enforcement falls disproportionately on complex high-income returns. Low- and middle-income households would not pay higher taxes directly, but honest ones indirectly bear more of the tax burden when others evade.

drawbacks.text: The restriction would have removed the main enforcement lever Congress had just funded; the IRS itself and Treasury said the Inflation Reduction Act's enforcement money was aimed at complex, high-income evasion rather than routine audits of wage earners.
The bill would not change any audit rates under existing IRS budgets, only the new money—so its headline protection was narrower than its framing suggested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the handful of taxpayers actually audited with new money, the benefit is a guaranteed shield; for everyone else the effect is that money meant to close the tax gap, which falls most heavily on evaders at the top, is restricted. On net, the bill trades a small, already-targeted audit risk for a real reduction in the government's ability to collect from people with the most sophisticated avoidance strategies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee from its referral on September 12, 2022 until the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with no vote, hearing, or floor action.

narrative.text: Introduced September 12, 2022 by Sen. Crapo with 14 original Senate cosponsors and 19 total Republican cosponsors, one day after the Inflation Reduction Act was signed into law.
Referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day of introduction; no further action of any kind is recorded for the remainder of the Congress.
The bill expired with the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 without receiving a committee vote or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income taxpayers and their advisers, who faced no change to audit risk because the bill never became law, and members of Congress who could point to having co-sponsored a popular-sounding protection without having to pass one. The Inflation Reduction Act's IRS funding went forward unchanged, so ordinary households saw no shift in audit policy either way from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and anyone avoiding audit risk

for.name: Mike Crapo
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-ID), bill sponsor and Ranking Member of the Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 4817 on September 12, 2022 to prohibit use of the new IRS funding for audits below $400,000.

for.name: 19 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors to the bill.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled it for a markup or vote during the rest of the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Republicans, including the 14 original Senate cosponsors on introduction; no Democrat cosponsored the bill.

industries.industry: High-income individuals and pass-through business owners
industries.note: These are the taxpayers most exposed to the 'army of auditors' framing and would be shielded, but most earn above the $400,000 line, so the bill's protection was largely symbolic for this group.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax advisory industry
industries.note: Firms that sell audit defense and avoidance planning benefit when audit activity and enforcement staffing are constrained, since enforcement gaps reduce risk for noncompliant clients.
Would have restricted how a recently appropriated $80 billion could be used, reducing the IRS's ability to narrow the tax gap with the money Congress had already approved.
